newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire copperbelt leader says Kabila unstoppable.
newsitem.headline: Zaire copperbelt leader says Kabila unstoppable.

text.p: The leader of the biggest party in Zaire's autonomy-hungry mining province of Shaba said on Thursday nothing would stop Laurent Kabila's rebels taking the province if the war went on.
Kyungu wa Kumwanza, Shaba's suspended governor, called on ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko to meet Kabila for talks but said they must also include regional leaders such as himself.
"The truth is, all the people here are waiting eagerly for Mr Kabila. They see him as a saviour," Kyungu told Reuters in the regional capital Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city.
"We can't stop him. If he comes, he will enter, with force if necessary. It's a sad fact that those who want to continue the war must face."
The rebels are some 400 km (250 miles) from Lubumbashi, but closing in on Kamina, a railway junction whose fall would cut Shaba from diamond-rich Kasai and the rest of Zaire.

Kyungu, 58, says peace talks should aim for a ceasefire and a national unity government that would oversee elections within three to six months, to end the country's transition to democracy that Mobutu has now dragged out for seven years.
He leads UFERI, the Union of Federalists and Independent Republicans, Shaba's most popular party which seeks autonomy for the province they call by its old name, Katanga.
"We control almost all of Katanga. There is no question of ignoring us. We must take part in talks, due to the importance of our party and our region of six million (people)," he said.
Shaba has a history of violent attempts to break away from Zaire that go back to independence from Belgium in 1960.
Kabila fought in them, but now he, like Kyungu, says Zaire must stay together but become a far less centralised state.
"Independence is out of the question because the international community would not accept it," Kyungu said.
UFERI wants the region to keep the lion's share of receipts from its mineral wealth which have until now gone to Kinshasa and, many believe, into the pockets of politicians.

Kyungu was suspended as governor in 1995 after allegations he tried to smuggle in arms to secede, but said parliament had just approved a motion to reinstate him that now awaited only Mobutu's signature. His successor was unavailable for comment.
Critics accuse Kyungu of enriching himself in power, like so many other officials under Mobutu, and his name is rumoured locally to be on a list of people Kabila refuses to deal with.

"We have had no contact with Kabila, we don't know what he really wants with us, so at first when he arrives we'll hide," said Kyungu, adding that he and fellow Katangan Kabila came from the same village of Ankoro, but had not met.

The biggest fear for the million residents of Lubumbashi, situated near the Zambian border 1,700 km (1,050 miles) from Kinshasa, is that Zairean troops will loot the town as they did before the jungle city of Kisangani fell at the weekend.
No one expects the army to stand and fight.

Some of the 1,000-plus Belgian, Lebanese and other expatriates working at copper and cobalt mines in Shaba have evacuated families. Many expect that in a couple of weeks Kabila will be in control of the southeastern province.

Many expatriates and local businessmen say they expect little trouble. Unlike Kisangani, Lubumbashi offers looting soldiers no obvious line of retreat due to its geographical position on a toe-shaped stretch of land jutting into Zambia.

Storekeepers who saw their businesses ravaged in the last army rampage in 1991 say soldiers have already started to desert their bases. Some have been disarmed by patrols from other units who have been ordered to keep things calm, they add.
